title: True, Believed, Justified, and Still Not Knowledge
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

intro.summary: Philosophers had long proposed a simple recipe for knowledge: you know something when it is true, you believe it, and you are justified in believing it. In a three-page paper, Gettier tests that recipe with two short made-up stories in which a man named Smith meets all three conditions. In both stories Smith's belief turns out true only by luck, through a fact he knows nothing about, so he plainly does not know it. Gettier concludes that the three conditions are not enough for knowledge. The paper shows what the recipe misses but does not say what should replace it, and its force rests on readers sharing the intuition that Smith does not know.
background: Epistemology is the branch of philosophy that asks what knowledge is and how we get it.
A 'proposition' is just a claim that can be true or false, such as 'Jones owns a Ford'.
A condition is 'sufficient' for something if meeting it guarantees that thing, so one case that meets the condition without the thing shows it is not sufficient.
A thought experiment is an imagined case built to test a general claim, much as a lab experiment tests a theory.
intro.aha: You can believe something true, have excellent reasons for it, and still not know it, because your reasons and the truth can be connected only by luck.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: What is the difference between knowing something and merely believing it? A popular answer, going back in some form to Plato, says knowledge is a belief that is true and that you have good reasons for. Philosophers such as Chisholm and Ayer wrote careful versions of this three-part recipe. Gettier asks whether the recipe really works.
primer.quote: attempts have been made in recent years to state necessary and sufficient conditions for someone's knowing a given proposition.

primer.heading: What he did
primer.body: Gettier first makes two quiet points. You can be justified in believing something false, because good evidence can still mislead you. And if you correctly reason from a justified belief to something it guarantees, the new belief is justified too. He then builds two short stories about a job-seeker named Smith, using these points to put Smith in a strange position.

primer.heading: What he found
primer.body: In each story Smith reasons well from strong but mistaken evidence. He reaches a conclusion that happens to be true, for reasons he knows nothing about. All three parts of the recipe are met: the belief is true, Smith believes it, and he is justified. Yet nobody would say he knows it, because he got lucky.
primer.quote: If these two conditions hold then Smith does not know that (h) is true, even though (i) (h) is true, (ii) Smith does believe that (h) is true, and (iii) Smith is justified in believing that (h) is true.

primer.heading: Why it matters
primer.body: Two tiny examples were enough to show that true, justified belief does not add up to knowledge. A recipe meant to guarantee knowledge fails if even one case meets it without knowledge. The paper sparked decades of attempts to find a missing fourth ingredient. It offers no fix itself, and it depends on readers agreeing that Smith lacks knowledge, an intuition most people, though not everyone, share.

concepts.title: The three-part recipe for knowledge
concepts.idea: The classic view says you know a claim exactly when it is true, you believe it, and you are justified in believing it, and a case missing any one part is not knowledge.

terms.means: A claim that can be true or false, such as 'the train leaves at 9:15'
A belief held for good reasons or strong evidence, not a guess or a hunch
Something that must be present: without it, there is no knowledge
Something that is enough: if it is present, there is knowledge

concepts.recap: The classic recipe: knowing P means P is true, you believe P, and you are justified in believing P. Each part is needed, and together they are meant to be enough.

understand.explanation: Philosophers have long asked what separates knowing something from merely believing it, and this 1963 paper tests one popular answer. That answer says a person S knows a proposition P (a claim that can be true or false) exactly when three things hold: P is true, S believes P, and S is justified in believing P. A justified belief is one that S holds for good reasons or strong evidence, not as a guess or a hunch. Each part is meant to be a necessary condition: if any one is missing, it is not knowledge. Together the three are meant to be a sufficient condition: if all three hold, that is enough for knowledge. Gettier notes that Plato seems to have considered such a definition, and that Chisholm and Ayer gave versions that used 'adequate evidence' and 'the right to be sure' in place of 'justified'.
understand.quote: (a) S knows that P IFF (i) P is true, (ii) S believes that P, and (iii) S is justified in believing that P.

activities.question: Before we start: what do you think it takes to really know something, rather than just believe it?

options.text: Being very sure of it
options.feedback: Many people start here. But people can be completely sure of things that are false, and false things can't be known. Keep this in mind as you meet the classic view.

options.text: Being right about it
options.feedback: Being right matters. But a lucky guess can be right too, and we don't usually call a lucky guess knowledge. The classic view adds more than this.

options.text: Being right, believing it, and having good reasons for it
options.feedback: This is close to the classic view you are about to meet. It joins truth, belief and good reasons into one recipe.

options.text: Having good reasons, whether or not you turn out to be right
options.feedback: Good reasons matter. But if the claim is false, most people would say you didn't know it, only thought you did. The classic view also requires truth.

activities.title: Running the recipe on one everyday case

steps.text: Maria says: 'The 9:15 train runs today.' This is our proposition P, a claim that can be true or false.
Ingredient (i): is P true? The 9:15 train does run today.
Ingredient (ii): does Maria believe P? Yes. She heads to the station at 9:00.
Ingredient (iii): is Maria's a justified belief? She checked the rail company's live timetable this morning, so she has good evidence.
All three are present, so the recipe says Maria knows the 9:15 runs today.
Now change one thing. Suppose Maria never checked anything and just had a feeling the train would run. It still runs and she still believes it, but she has no good reason.

activities.takeaway: To use the recipe, check each of the three ingredients one at a time. If any one is missing, the recipe says it is not knowledge.

activities.title: Which ingredient is missing?
activities.prompt: Each made-up case has at most one ingredient missing. Sort each case by the ingredient it lacks, or by 'all three present'.

cards.text: Ana picks a horse because it has a funny name and is sure it will win. It wins.
cards.feedback: The claim turned out true and Ana believed it, but a funny name is no reason at all. This is a lucky guess, so justification is missing.

cards.text: Ben reads on the pool's website that it opens at 7 and believes it. The hours changed yesterday: it now opens at 8.
cards.feedback: Ben believes it and had a reasonable source, but the claim is false. You can't know something that isn't so, so truth is missing.

cards.text: Chloe's blood test shows she is anaemic, and her doctor explains the results. Chloe refuses to believe it. She is anaemic.
cards.feedback: The claim is true and the evidence is strong, but Chloe doesn't believe it. Someone who rejects a claim doesn't know it, so belief is missing.

cards.text: Dev counts the chairs in the room himself: 12. He believes there are 12, and there are.
cards.feedback: True, believed, and backed by his own careful count. All three ingredients are present, so the recipe calls this knowledge.

cards.text: Eli dreams that his sister is expecting a baby and believes it when he wakes up. She is.
cards.feedback: True and believed, but a dream is not good evidence. Eli was right by luck, so justification is missing.

cards.text: Fatima has seen the bank statement showing her rent was paid, but she is too anxious to believe it went through. It did.
cards.feedback: The claim is true and she has the evidence in hand, but she doesn't believe it. Belief is missing.

cards.text: Gus reads the thermometer outside his window: 3°C. He believes it is cold outside, and it is.
cards.feedback: A working thermometer is good evidence, he believes it, and it's true. All three ingredients are present.

cards.text: Hana's usually reliable colleague tells her the meeting is in Room 4, so Hana believes it. The colleague misread the email: it's in Room 6.
cards.feedback: Hana believes it and trusted a normally reliable source, but the claim is false. Truth is missing.

hints: For each case, ask three questions in turn: Is the claim actually true? Does the person believe it? Do they have a good reason?
Watch for 'refuses to believe' or 'can't believe' (belief), lucky hunches or dreams (justification), and claims that turn out wrong (truth).
activities.takeaway: Each ingredient can go missing on its own, and in every such case we hesitate to call it knowledge. That is why the classic view treats each part as necessary.

activities.question: Look back at your first guess. According to the classic recipe, which combination is enough for someone to know a claim?

options.text: The claim is true and the person believes it
options.feedback: Not enough on the recipe. Ana's horse and Eli's dream were true and believed, but they were lucky guesses. Justification is also required.

options.text: The person believes it and has good reasons
options.feedback: Not enough on the recipe. Ben and Hana had reasons and believed, but the claims were false. Truth is also required.

options.text: The claim is true, the person believes it, and they are justified in believing it
options.feedback: Right. The classic recipe says these three together are sufficient for knowledge. Whether three really are enough is exactly what Gettier's paper goes on to question.

options.text: The claim is true and the person is very sure of it
options.feedback: Being sure is not the same as being justified. A dreamer can be very sure. The recipe needs good reasons, not just strong confidence.

concepts.title: Good reasons can still point the wrong way
concepts.idea: Being justified does not guarantee being right: strong evidence can support a belief that is in fact false.

terms.means: Evidence that gives strong, reasonable support to a claim that happens to be false

concepts.recap: Justification is about how good your reasons are, and truth is about how the world is. Excellent reasons can still back a false belief.

understand.explanation: Ravi did everything a sensible person could do, and his belief was still false. Being justified is about the quality of your reasons: how well your evidence supports the belief. Being true is about how the world actually is. These are two separate things, so they can come apart. When good evidence happens to support something false, we call it misleading evidence, and a person who trusts it is still justified. Gettier states this as the first of two starting points for his argument. He does not argue for it at length, because he takes it to be how we ordinarily use 'justified' when we talk about knowledge.
understand.quote: First, in that sense of 'justified' in which S's being justified in believing P is a necessary condition of S's knowing that P, it is possible for a person to be justified in believing a proposition that is in fact false.

activities.prompt: Two travellers both believe 'My train leaves at 9:15.' Both are wrong: it actually leaves at 9:40. Compare how each of them got to the belief.

cases.label: Maya: a careless false belief
cases.text: Maya half-remembers that 'trains are usually at quarter past.' She doesn't check anything. She believes her train leaves at 9:15. She is wrong, and she had no good reason to think it in the first place.

cases.label: Ravi: a well-supported false belief
cases.text: Ravi checks the official timetable that morning and looks at the station's departure board. He also asks a member of staff. All three say 9:15. Minutes later a schedule change moves the train to 9:40, and it hasn't been posted yet. Ravi believes his train leaves at 9:15. He is wrong too, but his reasons were excellent.

activities.takeaway: Both beliefs are false, yet they are not on the same footing. Maya had no grounds. Ravi had about the best grounds anyone could have. Strong reasons made his belief justified, and they still could not make it true.

activities.title: Justified or not, whatever the truth
activities.prompt: Sort each belief by whether the person had good reasons for it. The card also tells you whether the belief turned out true. Notice that truth doesn't decide where a card goes.

cards.text: Lena believes it will rain this afternoon. The forecast says 90% chance and the sky is full of dark clouds. It stays dry. (False)
cards.feedback: Justified. A reliable forecast plus what she can see are good reasons. The evidence pointed the wrong way this time, but that makes her belief false, not unjustified.

cards.text: Tom believes the coin will land heads because he 'feels lucky.' It lands heads. (True)
cards.feedback: Not justified. A lucky feeling is no evidence about a fair coin. Being right by chance doesn't give him good reasons after the fact.

cards.text: Ana believes her brother is home. His car is in the drive, the lights are on, and he just texted 'home now.' He is home. (True)
cards.feedback: Justified. Several independent signs support the belief, and here it is also true. Justified and true can go together. They just aren't guaranteed to.

cards.text: Sam believes a stock will double next month because an anonymous stranger in a chatroom said so. It falls. (False)
cards.feedback: Not justified. An unknown stranger's tip is not good evidence. This is a false belief with weak grounds, like Maya's train guess.

cards.text: A doctor diagnoses an infection. The textbook symptoms and a lab result all fit. A rare lab mix-up made the result wrong, and the patient has something else. (False)
cards.feedback: Justified. The doctor reasoned well from evidence that is normally trustworthy. That evidence was misleading, so the belief was false, yet the doctor was still justified.

cards.text: Priya has to name Australia's capital. She picks between Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra at random and says Canberra. She's right. (True)
cards.feedback: Not justified. A random pick among three options gives no real support, even though it landed on the truth.

hints: Ignore the (True) or (False) label at first. Ask only: did this person have good reasons?
A gut feeling, a random pick or an anonymous tip is not good evidence, even when it happens to be right.
Three cards belong in each group, and each group mixes true and false beliefs.
activities.takeaway: Each group holds both true and false beliefs. Whether you are justified depends on your reasons. Whether you are right depends on the world. Gettier needs exactly this gap: a person can have excellent reasons and still be wrong.

concepts.title: Sound reasoning passes justification along
concepts.idea: If you are justified in believing P and you correctly deduce Q from it, you are justified in believing Q, even if P later proves false.

terms.means: P entails Q when Q must be true whenever P is true: there is no way for P to hold and Q to fail.
To draw a conclusion by reasoning that follows strictly from what you started with, step by step.

concepts.recap: Correct reasoning hands justification on from a starting belief to its conclusion, and the conclusion stays justified even if the starting belief turns out false.

understand.explanation: Some claims are tied together so tightly that if the first is true, the second must be true too. Philosophers say the first claim entails the second. When you notice such a link and draw the second claim from the first, you deduce it. Gettier's second starting point is that this kind of careful reasoning passes justification along: if you were justified in believing the first claim, you are now justified in believing the second. Because justified beliefs can be false (the previous idea), the second belief stays justified even if the first later turns out to be false. Gettier does not prove this principle. He states it as one of two points he takes as given before presenting his cases.
understand.quote: Secondly, for any proposition P, if S is justified in believing P, and P entails Q, and S deduces Q from P and accepts Q as a result of this deduction, then S is justified in believing Q.

activities.title: Smith reasons from (d) to (e)

steps.text: Smith and Jones have both applied for the same job. The company president has assured Smith that Jones will be selected. Ten minutes ago, Smith counted the coins in Jones's pocket.
On that evidence Smith believes (d): 'Jones is the man who will get the job, and Jones has ten coins in his pocket.'

Look at what (d) commits you to. If Jones gets the job and Jones has ten coins, then whoever gets the job has ten coins. So (d) entails (e): 'The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.'
Smith notices this link and accepts (e) because of (d). He has deduced (e) from (d).
steps.result: Smith believes (e) on the grounds of (d).

steps.text: Gettier's verdict on this step: 'In this case, Smith is clearly justified in believing that (e) is true.' The justification that supported (d) now supports (e) as well.
Now recall that strong evidence can still support a false belief. Suppose (d) later proves false. That does not undo the justification Smith had for (e). He reasoned well from good evidence.

activities.takeaway: Justification runs from the evidence to (d), then across the correct deduction to (e). Each link must be sound. Whether (d) is actually true does not affect the chain.

activities.prompt: Trace the route by which Smith's justification reaches his belief in (e). Click the steps in order, starting where the justification comes from.

nodes.label: A lucky hunch about the winner

activities.explanation: Justification starts with Smith's evidence. That evidence supports (d), and Smith's correct deduction carries the support on to (e). Whether (e) is actually true is a separate question: truth is one of the three conditions for knowledge, but it is not where justification comes from. A lucky hunch gives no justification at all. Smith did not guess. He reasoned from evidence.

activities.question: Maria reads the official timetable, which says her train leaves at 9:05. She reasons: 'If it leaves at 9:05, it leaves before 10:00,' and so she believes her train leaves before 10:00. In fact the timetable had a misprint and the 9:05 time was wrong. Was Maria justified in believing her train leaves before 10:00?

options.text: Yes. She was justified in believing it leaves at 9:05, and she correctly deduced 'before 10:00' from that, so the justification carries over.
options.feedback: Right. An official timetable is good evidence, so the 9:05 belief was justified even though it was false. 'Leaves at 9:05' entails 'leaves before 10:00', and Maria drew the conclusion correctly. By Gettier's principle, the conclusion is justified too.

options.text: No. Her starting belief was false, so nothing she built on it can be justified.
options.feedback: This mixes up justification with truth. A false belief can still be justified when the evidence for it is good. Correct reasoning from a justified belief yields a justified conclusion, whether or not the starting belief turns out true.

options.text: Only if the train really does leave before 10:00.
options.feedback: Whether the conclusion is true is a separate condition from whether it is justified. Maria's justification comes from her evidence and her reasoning. It does not come from how things turn out at the station.

options.text: No. Deduction only works when you are certain of the starting point.
options.feedback: Gettier's principle asks only that she be justified in the starting belief, not certain of it. Strong evidence is enough to pass justification along through a correct deduction.

hints: Separate two questions: was the starting belief justified, and was the reasoning correct?
Does a misprint she could not have known about make her reliance on the official timetable unreasonable?

activities.question: Which of these people does Gettier's principle say is justified in the conclusion? Each is justified in the starting belief.

options.text: Ali is justified in believing 'It rained last night', and concludes 'The streets are flooded today.'
options.feedback: Rain last night does not entail flooded streets. The streets could be dry. Without an entailment, the principle does not pass the justification along.

options.text: Bea is justified in believing 'Sam is in Paris', and concludes 'Sam is in France.'
options.feedback: Correct. Being in Paris entails being in France, and Bea draws the conclusion from her justified belief. This is exactly the pattern Gettier describes.

options.text: Cal is justified in believing 'Sam is in France', and concludes 'Sam is in Paris.'
options.feedback: This runs the link backwards. Being in France does not entail being in Paris, since Sam could be in Lyon. The principle needs a real entailment, so it says nothing in Cal's favour.

options.text: Dee is justified in believing 'Sam is in Paris', and also believes 'Sam is in France', but only because a fortune teller told her so.
options.feedback: The entailment exists, but Dee did not accept the conclusion as a result of deducing it. Gettier's principle requires that S 'deduces Q from P and accepts Q as a result of this deduction.' Here the belief rests on the fortune teller.

hints: The principle needs two things: a real entailment, and a belief in the conclusion that actually comes from that reasoning.
For each option, ask whether the starting claim could be true while the conclusion is false.

concepts.title: Case I: the man with ten coins
concepts.idea: A belief about 'the man who will get the job' can be made true by a different man than the one the believer had in mind.

predict.question: A new twist on the story. Jones does get the job, just as the president said. But Jones spent a coin and now has 9. Smith, by chance, has 10 coins. Is (e), 'The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket', true?
options: Yes, because somebody in the story (Smith) has ten coins
No, because 'the man who will get the job' is now Jones, and he has 9
Yes, because Smith's evidence for it was strong
There is no way to tell
why: Tempting, because in Gettier's story Smith's ten coins did the work. But (e) is only about the winner's pocket. When Jones wins, Smith's coins stop mattering.
Right. 'The man who will get the job' picks out whoever actually wins. Here that is Jones, whose pocket fails the test, so (e) is false.
Strong evidence makes a belief justified, not true. You met this idea earlier: good reasons can point the wrong way.
The facts are fully given. Once you know who wins and how many coins he holds, (e) has a definite answer.

terms.means: A claim made of two parts joined by 'and'. It is true only if both parts are true.
A phrase like 'the man who will get the job' that picks out whoever fits it, whoever that turns out to be.

model.title: Smith's picture of the world beside the real world
model.note: Teaching model: Gettier's Case I reduced to three facts: who gets the job, Smith's coins and Jones's coins. In the grid, 1 means true and 0 means false. Smith's beliefs are fixed as the paper describes them. In the paper both men have exactly ten coins. Other coin counts are illustrative 'what ifs', not part of the paper.

controls.label: Smith really gets the job (off = Jones does)

rows.label: (d) Jones gets the job and has ten coins
Coins in the pocket of whoever gets the job
(e) The man who gets the job has ten coins

steps.say: This grid puts Smith's picture of the world on the left and the real world on the right. A 1 means true and a 0 means false.
This switch decides who really gets the job: Jones, or Smith himself.
This slider is how many coins are really in Smith's pocket. Smith has never counted them.
And this one is Jones's pocket. Smith counted ten coins there just minutes ago.
Back to the start. These boxes tell you which claims are true in the world you have set.

explore.prompt: Rebuild the trap yourself. Change the facts of the story and watch which claims survive.

goals.text: Make (e) true even though Jones's pocket no longer holds what Smith counted.
hints: If Jones's count is off and Jones still wins, can (e) be true? Who would have to win instead?
Hand the job to Smith, then look at whose pocket the 'whoever gets the job' row is reading.
Now Smith's own pocket has to satisfy claim (e) all by itself.

goals.text: Make (d) false while the job still goes to Jones, then see whether (e) survives.
hints: (d) has two parts. Which one can you break without changing who gets the job?
Leave the job switch alone and work on Jones's pocket.
Any count other than the one Smith made will do.

feedback.correct: Yes. (e) is about whoever actually gets the job. When Jones wins, only Jones's pocket counts, and 9 coins makes (e) false. Smith's ten coins are irrelevant.
feedback.incorrect: The phrase 'the man who will get the job' does not float free. It picks out the actual winner. In this twist the winner is Jones, so (e) is true only if Jones has ten coins, and he has 9.

steps.say: Start in the world Smith imagines. Jones gets the job and Jones has ten coins. Every line Smith believes is true.
(d) is a conjunctive proposition: two parts joined by 'and', so both must hold. From it Smith deduces (e), and as you saw earlier, that deduction passes his justification along.
Now change one fact Smith knows nothing about. Smith, not Jones, gets the job. The first part of (d) fails, so all of (d) collapses.
Look at (e). 'The man who will get the job' is a definite description: it points at whoever really wins. That is now Smith, so (e) is checked against Smith's pocket.
Smith's pocket holds five coins, so (e) is false here. Smith's careful count of Jones's coins plays no part any more.
Now give Smith ten coins, as Gettier's story does. (e) switches back to true.
Here is Gettier's world. (d), Smith's reason, is false. (e), his conclusion, is true, but only because of a pocket he never counted.

understand.explanation: Smith reasons from (d), 'Jones will get the job and has ten coins', to (e), 'the man who will get the job has ten coins'. Claim (e) never names Jones. It is about whoever gets the job. Gettier then fixes the facts so that Smith himself gets the job and happens to have ten coins too. (d) is false, but (e) comes out true, made true by Smith's pocket rather than the Jones-based evidence Smith relied on. Smith's belief in (e) is true, believed and justified, yet what makes it true has nothing to do with his reasons. This is an imagined case, not an observation. Its force rests on how clearly readers judge that Smith does not know (e).
understand.quote: But it is equally clear that Smith does not know that (e) is true; for (e) is true in virtue of the number of coins in Smith's pocket, while Smith does not know how many coins are in Smith's pocket, and bases his belief in (e) on a count of the coins in Jones's pocket, whom he falsely believes to be the man who will get the job.

connect.caption: The paper gives no formula. This is the model's rule written out. The job switch (blue) decides who the winner is. Jones's coins (Jones's colour) matter for (d) and, when Jones wins, for (e). Once Smith wins, only Smith's coins (green) decide (e). That is why (e) can be true while (d) is false.

concepts.recap: Claim (e) is about whoever gets the job, so Smith's own uncounted pocket can make it true while all his reasons were about Jones.

activities.prompt: Put the world Smith imagines beside the world Gettier actually describes. Which lines change, and which stay the same?

cases.label: The world as Gettier describes it

activities.takeaway: Line (e) reads true in both worlds, but for different reasons. In Smith's picture it rests on Jones's pocket. In reality it rests on Smith's own pocket, while (d), the claim Smith reasoned from, has collapsed.

concepts.title: Case II: the Ford and Barcelona
concepts.idea: An 'either…or' claim is true if either part is true, so a belief built on a false part can be made true by the other part, chosen at random.

predict.question: New case: from 'Jones owns a Ford', Smith also concludes 'Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown owns a boat.' Jones has no Ford, but Brown, unknown to Smith, does own a boat. What is Smith's belief in this new claim?
options: True, believed and justified, but not knowledge: the boat half makes it true
Not justified, because the claim Smith started from was false
Knowledge, because all three conditions are met
False, because Jones has no Ford
why: Right. This is the same shape as (h). The claim is true only through the half Smith never had evidence for, so his good reasons and the truth come apart.
Tempting, but sound reasoning from strong evidence passes justification along even when the starting claim turns out false. Smith is still justified.
All three conditions do hold, which is the point. Gettier's argument is that a case like this still is not knowledge, because the truth comes from a part Smith knows nothing about.
An either…or claim needs only one true half. The Ford half is false, but the boat half is true, so the whole claim is true.

terms.means: An 'either…or' claim. It is true when at least one of its halves is true.

model.title: Which half makes Smith's either…or claims true?
model.note: Teaching model: Brown can be in only one of four places, and each claim is simply true (1) or false (0). The three cities and the setup follow Gettier's Case II. The switch and slider are for exploring imagined worlds. They are not data.

controls.label: Where Brown really is (0 elsewhere, 1 Boston, 2 Barcelona, 3 Brest-Litovsk)

outputs.label: (f) Jones owns a Ford: true? (1 = yes)
Claims true only through the Brown half

columns: Ford half: Jones owns a Ford
Brown half: Brown is in this city

steps.say: Smith has strong evidence that Jones owns a Ford. From it he builds three 'either…or' claims about his friend Brown, one per row.
This switch sets whether Jones really owns a Ford, which is the part Smith has evidence for.
This slider moves Brown: elsewhere, Boston, Barcelona or Brest-Litovsk. Smith picked those cities at random and has no idea where Brown is.
The last column, and these boxes, say whether each whole claim comes out true. 1 means true, 0 means false.

explore.prompt: You are now in charge of the facts. Change what Jones owns and where Brown is, and watch which half of each claim is doing the work.

goals.text: Make Smith's evidence-backed claim (f) false while exactly one of his either…or claims still comes out true, and make that one not (h).
hints: Which half kept every claim true at the start? Take that support away first.
With the Ford half gone, only Brown's location can make a claim true.
Send Brown to a city named in one of the other two claims, not the one in (h).

goals.text: Make all three of Smith's either…or claims false at once.
hints: An either…or claim is false only when both of its halves are false.
Switch off the Ford half first, then look at where Brown is.
Brown has to be somewhere that none of the three claims names.

feedback.correct: Yes. The new claim works just like (h). Smith's justification flows from the Ford half, but the truth comes from the boat half, which he knows nothing about. All three conditions hold, yet it is not knowledge.
feedback.incorrect: The key is which half makes the claim true. An either…or claim needs only one true half. Smith stays justified because he reasoned soundly from strong evidence. Here the true half is the one his evidence says nothing about, so his belief is true by luck, not knowledge.

steps.say: Start in the world Smith thinks he is in. Jones owns a Ford and Brown is somewhere else. All three claims are true.
Each row is a disjunction: an either…or claim that is true when at least one half is true. Each half is called a disjunct. Here the Ford disjunct is true, so every row is true.
Move Brown around. Nothing changes. While Jones owns a Ford, Brown's location does no work at all.
Now Gettier's first twist. Jones does not own a Ford; he is driving a rented car. With Brown elsewhere, every claim collapses to false.
The second twist: by sheer coincidence, Brown really is in Barcelona.
(h) jumps back to true. But look at which disjunct carries it: the Brown half, the city Smith picked blindly.

So (h) is true, Smith believes it, and he is justified, since he reasoned soundly from strong evidence. Yet his evidence is about Fords, and the truth comes from Brown. That is the gap Gettier points to.

understand.explanation: From his strong evidence that Jones owns a Ford, Smith correctly infers three either…or claims, each pairing the Ford claim with a city he chose at random for Brown. A disjunction is true if at least one disjunct is, so while Jones owns a Ford all three are true wherever Brown is. Gettier then removes the Ford: Jones is driving a rented car. By sheer coincidence Brown really is in Barcelona, so (h) stays true, now through the half Smith picked blindly. Smith still believes (h) and is still justified, but what makes (h) true has nothing to do with his evidence, so Gettier says he does not know it. This is an imagined case, an argument by example, not an observation of real people.
understand.quote: And secondly, by the sheerest coincidence, and entirely unknown to Smith, the place mentioned in proposition (h) happens really to be the place where Brown is. If these two conditions hold then Smith does not know that (h) is true, even though (i) (h) is true, (ii) Smith does believe that (h) is true, and (iii) Smith is justified in believing that (h) is true.

check.task: Set up a world where Smith's belief (g), the Boston claim, is true, but only thanks to the Brown half and not his evidence.
check.hint: For the truth to come only from the Brown half, the Ford half has to be false. Then put Brown in the city that (g) names.
check.misconception: That a true either…or belief built on good evidence must be true because of that evidence. It can be true through the other half instead.

The orange part is the Ford half, the part Smith has evidence for, and it matches the switch. The Brown half matches the slider. The paper notes that each of (g), (h) and (i) is entailed by (f): if the Ford half is true, the whole claim is true.

concepts.recap: An either…or belief inferred from a false claim can still come out true through its other, randomly chosen half: true, believed and justified, but true by luck.

concepts.title: One counterexample breaks the recipe
concepts.idea: Because Smith meets all three conditions yet clearly does not know, true justified belief is not sufficient for knowledge, and the same holds for Chisholm's and Ayer's versions.

terms.means: A set of conditions that is always enough: whenever they all hold, the thing follows, with no exceptions
A single case where a general claim's conditions hold but its conclusion does not, which shows the claim is false

concepts.recap: You can believe something true, have excellent reasons for it, and still not know it, because your reasons and the truth can be connected only by luck.

understand.explanation: The classic recipe says that whenever a claim is true, believed and justified, you know it. That 'whenever' makes the recipe a sufficient condition: the three parts are supposed to always be enough. To refute a claim of that kind you need no statistics and no survey. One clear case where all three parts hold but knowledge is missing does the job, and such a case is called a counterexample. Gettier gives two: in each, Smith's belief is true, he holds it, and he deduced it correctly from strong evidence, yet what makes it true has nothing to do with his reasons. Chisholm's 'adequate evidence' and Ayer's 'right to be sure' play the same role as justification, so the same cases with small changes refute those versions too. The argument rests on the widely shared judgment that Smith does not know, and it shows only that the three parts are not enough, not that they are unneeded. Gettier offers no replacement recipe.
understand.quote: In our example, then, all of the following are true: (i) (e) is true, (ii) Smith believes that (e) is true, and (iii) Smith is justified in believing that (e) is true. But it is equally clear that Smith does not know that (e) is true

activities.question: Recall Case II. Smith has strong evidence that Jones owns a Ford. He picks 'Barcelona' at random and comes to believe: 'Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Barcelona.' Jones actually drives a rented car, but by sheer coincidence Brown really is in Barcelona. Does Smith know that his either-or claim is true?

options.text: Yes. The claim is true, he believes it, and he has good reasons.
options.feedback: That is exactly what the classic recipe would say. Keep this answer in mind: the next screens test whether those three facts really add up to knowledge here.

options.text: No. Something about how he got it right seems off.
options.feedback: Many people share this reaction. The next screens pin down what is off, and why it matters for the recipe as a whole.

options.text: I can't tell yet.
options.feedback: Fair enough. The next screens set out each part of the recipe against this case so you can decide.

activities.title: Hold the recipe up to both cases
activities.prompt: For each statement, decide whether it holds in Gettier's story or not.

cards.text: Case I: 'The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket' is true.
cards.feedback: It holds. Smith himself gets the job, and he happens to have ten coins in his pocket.

cards.text: Case I: Smith believes the man who will get the job has ten coins.
cards.feedback: It holds. He accepts it after seeing that it follows from his belief about Jones.

cards.text: Case I: Smith is justified in believing it.
cards.feedback: It holds. He deduced it correctly from a claim backed by the president's assurance and his own count of Jones's coins. Correct deduction passes justification along.

cards.text: Case I: The claim Smith reasoned from, 'Jones will get the job and has ten coins', is true.
cards.feedback: It does not hold. Jones does not get the job, so Smith's starting point is false, even though his evidence for it was strong.

cards.text: Case II: 'Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Barcelona' is true.
cards.feedback: It holds. An either-or claim needs only one true part, and Brown really is in Barcelona.

cards.text: Case II: Smith believes that either-or claim.
cards.feedback: It holds. He accepts it on the basis of his belief that Jones owns a Ford.

cards.text: Case II: Smith is justified in believing that either-or claim.
cards.feedback: It holds. He inferred it correctly from 'Jones owns a Ford', which his strong evidence supported. Gettier calls him 'completely justified'.

cards.text: Case II: Smith knows that Brown is in Barcelona.
cards.feedback: It does not hold. The paper says Smith 'has no idea where Brown is'. The place name was picked at random.

activities.takeaway: In both cases all three parts of the recipe hold. What fails is something the recipe never checks: the claim Smith actually reasoned from is false, and the part that is true got there by coincidence.
hints: Ask of each card: in the story as Gettier tells it, is this statement actually the case?
Truth, belief and justification are each met in both cases. Look for the cards about Smith's starting claim and about what he knows.

activities.prompt: Case II. Follow Smith's reasons arrow by arrow, from his evidence to his belief in the either-or claim (h). Then look at which box actually makes (h) true.
activities.explanation: Smith's reasons run from his Ford evidence through (f) to his belief in (h). That chain is well built, but it passes through a false claim. What actually makes (h) true is that Brown is in Barcelona, and no arrow runs from Smith's reasons to that box. The two chains meet only because Smith's random pick happened to match where Brown was. That gap, filled by luck, is why the true, justified belief is not knowledge.
hints: Start at Smith's evidence about Jones and follow only the arrows.
The random pick feeds into the belief, but it is not a reason Smith has. It is just how the sentence got its place name.

activities.question: Back to your first judgment. Smith's either-or claim is true, he believes it, and he is justified in believing it. What is the right verdict, and what does it do to the recipe?

options.text: He does not know it, so the recipe fails: all three parts can hold without knowledge, and one such case is enough to show they are not sufficient.
options.feedback: Right. The three parts hold, but Smith's reasons connect to the truth only by luck. A single clear counterexample shows the recipe is not a sufficient condition for knowledge. You can believe something true, have excellent reasons for it, and still not know it.

options.text: He knows it, because all three parts of the recipe hold.
options.feedback: This assumes the recipe is correct, which is the very thing being tested. What makes the claim true, Brown being in Barcelona, has nothing to do with Smith's reasons, so his getting it right is a coincidence. Gettier, and most readers, judge that this is not knowledge.

options.text: He does not know it, but only because he is not really justified.
options.feedback: Gettier rules this out. Being justified does not require being right, and correctly deducing a claim from something you are justified in believing passes justification along. Smith did exactly that, so the justification part holds.

options.text: He does not know it, but this refutes only the simple recipe, not Chisholm's or Ayer's.
options.feedback: Gettier says the same cases, with appropriate changes, refute those versions too. Strong evidence for a false claim also gives 'adequate evidence' and a 'right to be sure', so the same luck gap appears.

hints: Check each part of the recipe against the sort you just did.
Ask whether Smith's reasons have anything to do with where Brown actually is.
